## Grammar

Basic word order is SOV; it has postpositions. In the noun phrase: genitive order varies; noun before the adjective; demonstrative before the noun; numeral order varies; noun before the relative clause. Overall it is head-final.
It has no definite article, no indefinite article, a few cases, ergative-absolutive alignment, no grammatical number, a system of noun classes.
Verbs mark past, future, perfective and habitual; there are no evidentials. Negation uses a negator after the verb; yes/no questions use intonation alone. Verbs do not agree with their arguments.
Other features: pronouns can be dropped; alienable and inalienable possession told apart; serial verbs; verb reduplication; a copula; a periphrastic causative; no passive; question words moved to the front.
Measured morphology: 12 live grammatical markers, mean bondedness 0.7 (0 free word … 3 fused), 4 paradigm cells, 4 of them with allomorphy.

### Grammar sketch

Built from the typology and the live markers above (planet/language/sentences.py); where the engine tracks no marker for a construction, the form is the word such markers commonly grow from, and the text says so. Examples are glossed by the Leipzig rules (abbreviations under Sample sentences).

**Number.** Nouns do not mark number: one noun form serves for one or many; a numeral or 'many' says how many.

**Case.** Nouns take 1 case marker: ergative (ERG): a clitic after the noun phrase (t̪ʰu‼, from the genitive marker). Alignment is ergative: the subject of a transitive verb is marked (ERG); the subject of an intransitive verb and the object are not.

**Gender and noun classes.** Nouns fall into noun classes by meaning: class 1 for a single person, a clitic after the noun (nɛ‼ɭ, from 'person'); class 2 for people (plural of persons), a separate word before the noun (n‼ɪ, from 'people'); class 3 for languages, ways and tools, a prefix (kə, from 'tongue'); class 4 for lands, qualities and abstractions, and for every noun no other class takes, a clitic before the noun (te, from 'name').

| --- |
| CL4=day |

‘day’

**Tense and aspect.** Verbs mark tense and aspect. Past (PST): a clitic after the verb (i‼; ji‼ after a front or central vowel; from 'yesterday'); perfect (PRF): a separate word after the verb (o˯law‼, from 'finish'); future (FUT): a separate word after the verb (j‼a, from 'go'); habitual (HAB): a clitic after the verb (ra, from 'know'). Unmarked: progressive (left to context).

| *j‼aʃi=ji‼* |
| --- |
| go=PST |

‘(it) went’

| *j‼aʃi* | *o˯law‼* |
| --- | --- |
| go | PRF |

‘(it) has gone’

| *j‼aʃi* | *j‼a* |
| --- | --- |
| go | FUT |

‘(it) will go’

**Mood and evidentiality.** No evidential or mood marker is live; statements are unmarked.

**Person agreement.** Verbs do not agree with the subject. Short unstressed pronouns stand beside the verb (2SG ti‼), on their way to becoming agreement.

**Negation.** Negation is a clitic after the verb phrase (cʰa, from 'nothing').

| *ɔθ=t̪ʰu‼* | *te=ju‼* | *ʃikʰtʃip=cʰa* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG=ERG | CL4=milk | drink=NEG |

‘I do not drink the milk.’ (sentence 6 below)

**Questions.** Yes/no questions use rising intonation alone. Question words move to the front: who ɨ, what hi‼tʃʰij‼, where hi‼tʃʰj‼ɨkʰu‼, when lu, how ra‼.

| *ti‼=t̪ʰu‼* | *te=dʒe* | *a* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2SG=ERG | CL4=thunder | hear |

‘Do you hear the thunder?’ (sentence 4 below)

| *hi‼tʃʰij‼* | *i‼l‼tʰi=nɛ‼ɭ=t̪ʰu‼* | *l‼e‼tʃi* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| what | child=CL1=ERG | bring |

‘What does the child bring?’ (sentence 5 below)

**Commands.** There is no imperative marker: a command is the bare verb stem, with no subject and no subject or tense marker.

| *te=jep* | *tʰihil* |
| --- | --- |
| CL4=fish | eat |

‘Eat the fish!’ (sentence 12 below)

**Possession.** The possessor stands before the possessed noun, with no marker. Kin and body parts (inalienable) take no genitive marker. 'Having' is said with 'with' ('my mother is with a boat').

| *nɛ‼ɭ=nɛ‼ɭ* | *te=w‼ɔ‼j‼* |
| --- | --- |
| man=CL1 | CL4=dog |

‘the man's dog’

| *ɔθ* | *n‼ä=nɛ‼ɭ* | *te=hi‼haw* | *nu‼l* | *t̪ʰu‼* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1SG | mother=CL1 | CL4=boat | with | COP |

‘My mother has a boat.’ (sentence 7 below)

**Relative clauses.** Relative clause after the noun, introduced by the word for 'that' (as English that and German der grew from a pointing word).

| *o˯=nɛ‼ɭ* | *riʃɖiʃ* | *lɪtʰn‼ɪtɨh* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| woman=CL1 | REL | dance |

‘the woman who dances’

**Copula.** The copula is a separate word after the verb phrase (t̪ʰu‼, from 'that').

| *riʃɖiʃ* | *nɛ‼ɭ=nɛ‼ɭ* | *a=nɛ‼ɭ* | *t̪ʰu‼* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| that | man=CL1 | merchant=CL1 | COP |

‘That man is a merchant.’ (sentence 9 below)

| *te=hi‼kʰθil* | *ə‼t* | *t̪ʰu‼* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| CL4=water | cold | COP |

‘the water is cold’

**Reduplication.** Verbs reduplicate for an action done again and again, or by many (ITER), by copying the stem's last consonant and vowel after it.

| *j‼aʃi-ʃi* |
| --- |
| go-ITER |

‘(an action done again and again, or by many)’

| *nɛ‼ɭ=nɛ‼ɭ=t̪ʰu‼* | *te=jep* | *dʒaliː-liː* |
| --- | --- | --- |
| man=CL1=ERG | CL4=fish | hit-ITER |

‘The man hits the fish again and again.’ (sentence 14 below)

**Serial verbs.** Verbs can be strung together in one clause with one subject (serial verbs): 'take X come' is 'bring'. 'Go' after a motion verb gives its direction ('run go' = run away).

| *nɛ‼ɭ=nɛ‼ɭ=t̪ʰu‼* | *te=jep* | *ra‼h* | *ni* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| man=CL1=ERG | CL4=fish | take | come |

‘The man brings the fish (takes it and comes).’ (sentence 13 below)

| *hɔ‼* | *j‼aʃi* |
| --- | --- |
| run | go |

‘run away’

**Giving (two objects).** No dative: a serial construction, 'take the thing, give (it to) the person'.

| *o˯=nɛ‼ɭ=t̪ʰu‼* | *te=jep* | *ra‼h* | *i‼l‼tʰi=nɛ‼ɭ* | *o˯* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| woman=CL1=ERG | CL4=fish | take | child=CL1 | give |

‘The woman gives the child a fish.’ (sentence 11 below)

**Numerals.** Counting is restricted: a few number words, then hands and persons ('two hands' for ten), and 'many' past twenty. Twenty is nɛ‼ɭj‼ə‼d̪ and a hundred is ra‼n‼i.

| *j‼ə‼d̪j‼ɨnhɨj‼* |

| *lu‼j‼ə‼nhu* |
| --- |

‘15 = 10 + 5 ('ten' and 'five')’

**Linking clauses.** Complement clauses stand bare, with no complementizer.

| *nɛ‼ɭ=nɛ‼ɭ* | *te=w‼ɔ‼j‼* | *urut̪ʰ* | *j‼eiho˯* |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

‘The man says that the dog sleeps.’ (sentence 15 below)

**Demonstratives.** Demonstratives count two distances: 'this' u (near) and 'that' riʃɖiʃ (far).

| --- | --- |

‘that dog’

**Comparison.** An 'exceed' comparison: 'A is big, exceeds B', with the verb for 'climb' (as Yoruba ju 'exceed', Thai kwaa 'cross over').

| man=CL1 | big | COP | CL4=dog | exceed |

‘The man is bigger than the dog.’ (sentence 16 below)

### Families a speaker feels

The roots a speaker still feels: a derivation or compound younger than 3 kyr whose parts are still in use (per-word `roots`). 5 families of 3+ words; 9% of the 727 words share a root with another word.

The largest: **mother** *n‼ä* (N, coined 20 kyr ago in the blue dragon proto-language); 4 words have it as their main root, 4 contain it.

## Names of people and places

**Naming tradition.** Given names are two themes from a closed pool, compounded (as Germanic *Wil-helm*, Slavic *Vladi-mir*); the byname is the mother's name in the genitive with 'son' or 'daughter'. The tradition goes back to the blue dragon proto-language. Themes: first bear, friend, love, people, red, shine, spear, white; second fighter, heart, light, mind, peace, strong.

| **Rrirhhtenrree** | /r‼i‼htenrɛː/ | 'friend-mind' | old | Rrirhhtenrree 'friend-mind': rrirhhi 'friend' + tenlee 'mind'; an old name, coined in d48 4.0 kyr ago as Rrirhhitenlee |
| **Tatshrrerh** | /tatsʰr‼ɛ‼/ | 'love-strong' | old | Tatshrrerh 'love-strong': tatsh 'love' + rrerh 'strong'; an old name, coined in d48 4.0 kyr ago as Tatshrrerh |
| **Hukhal** | /hukʰaɻ/ | 'white-fighter' | new | Hukhal 'white-fighter': hu 'white' + khal 'fighter'; coined from today's words |
| **Tilrhïlrhrrï** | /til‼ɨl‼rɨ/ | 'red-light' | new | Tilrhïlrhrrï 'red-light': ti 'red' + lrhïlrhrrïlrhïlrh 'light'; coined from today's words |
| **Rrirhhlrhïlrhrrï** | /r‼i‼hl‼ɨl‼rɨ/ | 'friend-light' | new | Rrirhhlrhïlrhrrï 'friend-light': rrirhhi 'friend' + lrhïlrhrrïlrhïlrh 'light'; coined from today's words |
| **Lrhïlrhlïlrhïlrhrrï Rrirhhteshi** | /l‼ɨl‼lɨl‼ɨl‼rɨ r‼i‼hteʃi/ | 'shine-light, son of friend-mind' | matronymic | the mother's name Rrirhhtenrree + shi 'son' (compounded: the language has no genitive marker) |
| **Rrirhhtenrree Tatshrrerhtekh** | /r‼i‼htenrɛː tatsʰr‼ɛ‼tekʰ/ | 'friend-mind, daughter of love-strong' | matronymic | the mother's name Tatshrrerh + tekh 'daughter' (compounded: the language has no genitive marker) |

**Settlements.** **Ilrrili** /ilrili/ (town, 3,395): 'the black town'; named by the gnome (d509) who founded it 4.2 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Kikpitu** /kikpitu/ (village, 1,700): 'the big fence'; named by the halfling (d381.1) who founded it 1.7 kyr ago, kept as heard; **Huyti** /hujti/ (village, 1,678): 'the high field'; named by the halfling (d381.1) who founded it 1.7 kyr ago, kept as heard.

## Sample sentences

Built from this language's own words, word order, markers and agreement (planet/language/sentences.py). Each has the form line (‘-’ an affix boundary, ‘=’ a clitic boundary), a morpheme-by-morpheme gloss, the free translation, then the whole sentence in IPA (after the simple joining rules: a glide between two vowels, a nasal taking the place of a following stop) and in the book spelling. Nothing here is attested speech; it is what the grammar data implies.

## Texts

Each sentence in four lines: the book spelling, the IPA with its morph breaks, the gloss, and the English.

### A fable: The Bird and the Fish

One fixed short fable, told in every language as August Schleicher told his in Proto-Indo-European (1868), so that the same text shows what sound change and grammar change did. English: A bird sat in a tree. The bird saw a fish in the water. The bird said: “Come! I will give you a good seed.” The fish said: “I do not eat seeds. You will eat me.” The fish did not come. The bird ate the seed.
